description: We are a multidisciplinary team united by curiosity and a desire to turn ideas into something real. Each of us brings a different perspective, with interests spanning programming, AI, engineering, biology, health, and space exploration. We challenge each other, explore unconventional ideas, and learn beyond our fields. Together, we aim to combine our skills and curiosity to create meaningful and innovative solutions.
summary:
HALO (Health Autonomic Longevity in Orbit) is a web application designed to monitor crew health on long-duration, deep-space missions where communication with Earth is delayed.

We developed a dual-view platform featuring an astronaut interface with an interactive 3D body hologram and an Earth Command Center for flight surgeons. HALO addresses the challenge by centralizing fragmented data—including wearable ring metrics, spacecraft sensors (radiation and cabin CO2), and daily check-ins—into a single database. Built-in analytical and diagnostic engines evaluate these metrics against medical thresholds to safely flag spaceflight hazards and provide actionable, NASA-protocol-based guidance.

This project is important because deep-space exploration exposes astronauts to severe physiological risks. By enabling early anomaly detection, supporting crew autonomy, and bridging the information gap between spacefarers and ground control, HALO keeps astronauts safe, healthy, and performing at their peak far beyond Earth's reach.
details:
• What does it do or how does it work? HALO (Health Autonomic Longevity in Orbit) is a health-monitoring web application designed for astronauts on long deep-space missions and for flight surgeons on Earth. It centralizes data from wearable rings, spacecraft sensors (such as radiation and cabin $\text{CO}_2$), and astronaut daily check-ins into a single shared database. A built-in health and diagnosis engine checks these readings against medical thresholds and cross-references them with symptoms to flag potential spaceflight conditions (like sleep strain, radiation exposure, or possible decompression sickness) without making definitive unconfirmed diagnoses. It features two synchronized views: an astronaut view featuring an interactive 3D body hologram that highlights troubled areas in yellow or red with actionable NASA-protocol steps, and an Earth Command Center where flight surgeons can view fleet-wide status, open read-only mirrors of astronaut screens, and send directives.
    • Spots small health shifts early (e.g., compounding sleep debt or rising resting heart rate) before they become critical emergencies.
    • Reduces mission reliance on constant, delayed communication links with Earth.
    • Ensures serious health issues stand out immediately instead of getting lost in averages or hidden by otherwise normal metrics (enforced by health score caps when body zones turn red).
    • Establishes perfect situational awareness alignment, as astronauts and ground doctors see the exact same body hologram and underlying evidence.
    • Maintains clinical honesty by clearly separating confirmed data from conditions that require further medical imaging (labeled as "needs confirmation").
  • What is the intended impact of the project? To provide a reliable, autonomous baseline for crew health management on deep-space missions to the Moon and Mars. By keeping astronauts safe, informed, and performing at their peak, HALO aims to safeguard long-duration spacefarers against the physiological hazards identified by NASA's Human Research Program.
    • Backend: Node.js, Express, and SQLite.
    • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js (for rendering the 3D body model).
    • AI Guidance (Optional): Gemini AI SDK, used to generate supplemental briefings in the diagnostics panel.
    • Hardware: None. Wearable rings, radiation sensors, cabin $\text{CO}_2$ sensors, and blood-test analyzers are simulated.
    • Sources/References: NASA Human Research Program hazard/risk pages and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) radiation monitoring articles.
    • It merges acute spaceflight medical protocols with a modern longevity framework (inspired by Bryan Johnson’s Blueprint approach, scoring sleep, heart health, recovery, radiation, and mood on a 0–100 scale).
    • It uses a unique health-score capping mechanic where an astronaut's overall score cannot look healthy if vital body zones are flagged red (capping at 75 for 1–2 red zones and 65 for 3+), preventing a high score from masking severe localized issues.
    • It combines automated diagnostic logic with an interactive 3D human body atlas, turning dry numerical logs into an intuitive spatial diagnostic tool.
    • Autonomy vs. Control: Balancing astronaut self-sufficiency in deep space with oversight capabilities for ground-based flight surgeons.
    • Medical Integrity and Transparency: Ensuring the app never oversteps its bounds—explicitly labeling rules that are pending verification and marking unconfirmable conditions (like microgravity-related blood clots or vision changes) as "possible" or "missing evidence" rather than claiming a false positive diagnosis.
    • Unified Data Pathways: Designing the system architecture so that simulated demo data and incoming real-world wearable data (such as an actual Oura Ring) flow through the exact same ingestion pipeline.
